title: Feedback that changes what people do

audience.who: corporate employees giving feedback to peers and reports, many without formal management training
audience.knows: that feedback matters; has given and received vague praise and vague criticism; has felt a talk go well that changed nothing
audience.cares_about: not damaging working relationships, not wasting an awkward conversation, seeing the thing actually improve

outcome: Before their next feedback conversation, the viewer can turn a vague reaction ("that meeting was a mess") into feedback that names a specific observed behaviour, its effect, and one concrete next step the other person agrees to, and can tell which kind they just gave.
through_line: Feedback changes behaviour only when the other person leaves knowing exactly what they did, why it mattered, and what to do differently next time; warmth helps it land, but specificity and a next step are what make it stick.

arc_plan.what: A colleague gets a friendly, vague comment after a messy meeting, nods, feels fine, and repeats the same behaviour next week: the talk felt good and nothing changed.
arc_plan.source_anchor: knowledge: why vague feedback fails to change behaviour

arc_plan.what: Name the gap the viewer just watched (feelings changed, behaviour did not) and promise a way to close it in their next conversation.
arc_plan.source_anchor: knowledge: feedback aimed at behaviour vs at the person

arc_plan.what: Contrast feedback about the person or a general impression with feedback about an observable action, using the same colleague and the same meeting.

Rebuild the vague comment step by step on the running example: the specific situation and behaviour seen, the effect it had, then a concrete next step agreed together, each part visibly added to the same message.
arc_plan.source_anchor: knowledge: an established structured feedback model (e.g. situation, behaviour, impact) and the role of a forward-looking next step

arc_plan.what: Show why timing and a two-way check matter: feedback given close to the event, and asking how the other person sees it, so the next step is theirs and not only the giver's.
arc_plan.source_anchor: knowledge: prompt timing and dialogue in effective feedback

arc_plan.what: The viewer sees a few short feedback lines from a different workplace moment and decides which one would actually change behaviour, and what the others are missing.
arc_plan.source_anchor: knowledge: the elements established in the build

arc_plan.what: The viewer picks one real conversation they owe someone this week and drafts it in the rebuilt shape before they have it.
arc_plan.source_anchor: knowledge: the elements established in the build

arc_plan.what: Return to the same colleague and the next meeting after the rebuilt feedback: the specific behaviour has changed, and the relationship is intact.
arc_plan.source_anchor: knowledge: outcomes of specific, behaviour-focused feedback

must_cover.what: Why vague or general feedback (praise or criticism) tends not to change behaviour
Describe the observable behaviour in a specific situation, not the person's character or intent
State the effect or impact of that behaviour on work, people or results
End with a concrete, agreed next step or request for what to do differently
Give feedback soon after the event and make it a two-way conversation
Specific positive feedback also changes behaviour: it tells people what to keep doing

must_avoid: the sandwich method presented as best practice, unless the knowledge sheet supports it
statistics or percentages without a source on the approved sheet
invented sayings or attributions presented as real
a tour of feedback models one after another; one structure, used on one running example
a teacher's or HR-policy tone; no lecturing, no moralising about kindness
opening by explaining what feedback is, or with an agenda
harsh, humiliating or legal/disciplinary scenarios; this is everyday work feedback
on-screen character names that imply a real person or company
example_posture: One running example the whole lesson returns to: two colleagues of roughly equal standing on an ordinary team (a meeting that overran, a handover that missed details), neutral industry, low stakes, recognisable to anyone in an office or on a hybrid team. The check uses a different everyday moment so the viewer transfers, not recalls. Include one positive case so feedback is not only correction.
visual_direction: Warm story-cartoon people from the lesson's designed cast acting the moment out: faces that show the nod-and-forget of the vague version and the real shift after. One message that visibly grows as each part is added (behaviour, effect, next step), the same object across the build. A before and after of the same meeting. The repeated behaviour shown happening again, then not happening. Keep the presenter for the opening promise and the closing return at most; let the scenes carry the teaching.
voice_note: A mentor who has had these conversations and fumbled a few: warm, direct, a little wry about how good a vague chat can feel. Speaks to a capable peer, never to a pupil; short sentences, no jargon, no lecturing about kindness.
open_questions: Should the running example be peer-to-peer or manager-to-report? The brief assumes peers so it suits everyone; the requester may prefer a manager lens.
Is a named structured model (for example situation, behaviour, impact) wanted on screen by name, or only its parts? Depends on what the knowledge sheet supports.
Any organisational feedback framework the company already uses that the lesson should align with?
